title: One-click symmetry plane for flow and heat
body:
## Current behaviour

Halving a symmetric model is possible today: a slip wall for the flow plus an adiabatic face for heat on the fluid
domain, and a matching cut for the solids. But it takes several separate settings, and the solid side needs its own
treatment.

## What to build

A single **symmetry plane** condition for a fluid domain face that applies, together:
- zero normal velocity and zero shear (slip) for the flow;
- zero normal heat flux for the fluid and for any conducting solid cut by the plane;
- a check that the geometry and inputs are actually symmetric about the plane, with a warning if not.

Results can be mirrored for display, and derived totals (heat rate, flow) can optionally be doubled, clearly labelled.

## Verification

- A symmetric heated channel solved whole and as a half with the symmetry plane: fields and doubled totals agree
  within a stated tolerance.
- An asymmetric input triggers the warning.

Part of #697.

title: Parameter studies over model inputs with tabulated derived results
body:
## Current behaviour

Comparing designs (fin spacing, inlet velocity, fan choice, heat load) means editing the model and re-solving by hand
for each value, then collecting the numbers manually.

## What to build

A **parameter study**:
- Choose one or more model parameters: a dimension from the geometry or an input such as inlet velocity, power or a
  material choice.
- Give a list or range of values. Each point solves in turn, or in parallel where resources allow, with the usual solve
  caps.
- Each point records the derived results from #837 (heat rate, pressure drop, outlet temperatures, maximum solid temperature)
  and the validity and acceptance report.
- Output is a table and CSV, plus an XY plot of any result against the parameter.
- A failed or invalid point is shown as such and doesn't stop the study.

## Verification

- A study over the inlet velocity of a heated channel: the recorded heat rate and pressure drop match individual
  solves.
- A forced failure at one point is reported and the rest complete.

Part of #697; the fin-spacing comparison in #701 relies on it.

title: Guided setup for conjugate heat-transfer models
body:
## Current behaviour

A heat-transfer model with flow and solids is built from several separate commands:
- fluid domain;
- fluid material;
- obstacle bodies and their solid materials;
- inlets, outlets and walls;
- heat sources and thermal faces;
- a fluid step and its settings.

It's easy to miss a piece, and new users don't know the order.

## What to build

A guided setup that walks through those steps in order, with sensible defaults and a check at the end:
1. Pick the bodies that are fluid regions and the bodies that are solids.
2. Assign materials, from the library (#838) or custom.
3. Mark inlets (velocity or flow rate, temperature), outlets and walls.
4. Add heat sources (power per body) and thermal faces.
5. Choose the resolution, with a cell-count and run-time estimate before solving.
6. Run the model check, then offer to solve.

Every step is an ordinary command, so a script can do the same thing. The guided setup only sequences them and never
does anything a command can't. It can also start from a saved example, such as the electronics or exchanger samples.

## Verification

- A scripted run of the setup produces the same model as the equivalent command sequence.
- The final check catches each missing piece: no inlet, no material, unpowered solids, and an over-cap cell count.

Part of #697; supports the tutorials in #701.

title: Radiation to ambient from solid surfaces
body:
## Current behaviour

Solid surfaces lose heat only by conduction into the fluid, or through held-temperature and heat-flux faces. In still
or slow air, radiation from a heat sink or enclosure is often comparable to convection. Leaving it out over-predicts
temperatures.

## What to build

A **radiation to ambient** condition on solid surfaces:
- Inputs: a surface emissivity (0–1) and an ambient radiation temperature.
- Net flux: q = ε σ (T⁴ − T_amb⁴), applied on exposed solid faces of conducting bodies.
- The temperature dependence is handled stably (linearised per step or treated implicitly) and works in steady and
  transient runs.
- Results report radiated power per face set, and include it in the energy balance (#837).
- Surface-to-surface view factors are out of scope for this issue and are refused or documented as not modelled.

## Verification

- A lumped body cooling by radiation alone: temperature history against the analytic solution.
- A plate with combined convection and radiation: steady temperature against a hand calculation.
- The energy balance includes the radiated power.

Part of #697.

title: Thermal and fluid material library with temperature-dependent properties
body:
## Current behaviour

The material library (#99) covers structural metals. Thermal material properties are listed as coming soon. Heat
transfer between flow and solids needs, for every model:
- the fluid's density, viscosity, conductivity and specific heat;
- the solid's conductivity, specific heat and density.

Users currently type these in by hand.

## What to build

Library entries with cited sources (handbook or standard reference data, with the citation in the entry and a row in
the attribution list where required):
- **Fluids:** water, air, and a common water/glycol coolant mix. Properties are temperature-dependent over a stated
  range, as a table or fit, with the valid range enforced or warned about.
- **Solids:** aluminium alloys (e.g. 6061, 6063), copper, carbon and stainless steel, brass, FR-4 (orthotropic
  conductivity), borosilicate and silica glass, and a typical thermal interface material.

Entries can be picked with one click in the material dialog and by name in commands. A model saves the values it used,
so results don't change if the library is updated.

## Verification

- Each entry's values match its cited source at tabulated points.
- Interpolation inside the range and the warning outside it are tested.
- A natural-convection oracle case gives the same answer with library air as with hand-entered values.

Part of #697.

title: Derived heat-exchanger results: heat rate, face averages, pressure drop, duty and energy balance
body:
## Current behaviour

Fluid results can be shown as slices, streamlines and signed wall heat per area, but there are no commands for the
numbers a heat-exchanger study reports. The exchanger tutorials in #701 assume them.

## What to build

Read-only results commands, available from the GUI, CLI, scripts and the control channel:
- **Heat rate** through a named face set or surface (W), split into conduction and advection where meaningful.
- **Face averages** at a named face: area-averaged and mass-flow-weighted temperature, and area-averaged pressure and
  velocity.
- **Mass and volume flow** through a face.
- **Pressure drop** between two named faces.
- **Exchanger summary:** for a hot and a cold stream, the heat duty, both inlet and outlet temperatures, effectiveness
  and log-mean temperature difference.
- **Energy balance:** heat in through inlets, faces and sources against heat out, plus storage, with the residual as a
  fraction. This shows whether a result is converged and closed.

Results come as a table and CSV, with units, and say which time window they average over for unsteady runs. They are
reported as measurements, not validation.

## Verification

- A heated channel with analytic heat input: the energy balance closes to the stated tolerance, and outlet mean
  temperature matches the energy balance.
- Poiseuille flow: the pressure drop matches the analytic value.
- Synthetic fields with known integrals.

Part of #697; used by #701.

title: Thin conducting walls and internal baffles between fluid regions
body:
## Current behaviour

A conducting wall between two fluid regions has to be a voxelised solid, so its thickness has to be resolved by
lattice cells. Real heat-exchanger walls (tube walls, plate fins, separator sheets) are 0.1–1 mm thick, while the
passages either side are millimetres to centimetres wide. Resolving the wall sets the cell size for the whole domain.
For the coupled air/coolant exchanger in #700, that makes the run far more expensive than the flow needs.

## What to build

A **thin wall** (baffle): a zero-thickness sheet defined on a face set or surface, placed inside a fluid domain.
- **Flow:** it acts as a no-slip (or slip) wall on both sides, separating the passages either side. Fluid can't cross
  it.
- **Heat:** it conducts through its thickness with a user-given thickness and conductivity (or a conductance per area,
  W/m²K), plus optional in-plane conduction along the sheet.
- **Results:** temperature and heat flux are reported separately on each side, so the side-to-side difference is
  visible.
- **Coupling:** it works with the existing conducting solids, component power and thermal contact resistance (#677),
  and on both the CPU and GPU paths, or refuses clearly where unsupported.

## Verification

- A plane wall between two counter-flowing channels: overall heat-transfer coefficient and outlet temperatures against
  the analytic two-stream solution.
- The same wall resolved as a voxelised solid at high resolution, matched within a stated tolerance.
- Zero conductance must give zero heat crossing the wall to round-off.

Part of the heat-exchanger workflow in #697; needed for #700.

title: [Feature Request] Modern, workflow-first UI/UX inspired by SimScale
body:
### Current behaviour

FieldCraft is an incredibly promising project, and I genuinely appreciate the ambition to create a fully open-source, local-first engineering simulation platform.

However, in my opinion, its current interface still follows many of the traditional design conventions found throughout engineering simulation software.

This isn't exclusively an open-source problem. Even expensive, industry-standard CAE applications often rely on dated interface conventions, dense toolbars, deeply nested menus, and workflows that feel unnecessarily complicated by modern software design standards.

I recognize that FieldCraft has already received substantial UI/UX improvements, including those introduced in v0.6. My suggestion concerns the broader visual design philosophy and overall user experience, rather than any single missing feature or usability bug.

One example of a different approach is SimScale, which demonstrates how sophisticated engineering software can be presented through a cleaner, more modern, and visually coherent interface.

### What you need and why

I'd love to see FieldCraft explore a more ambitious, workflow-oriented UI/UX direction, taking inspiration from modern simulation platforms such as [[SimScale](https://www.simscale.com/)](https://www.simscale.com/).

As an aerospace engineering student, I believe that an intuitive, visually polished simulation environment can significantly improve both accessibility and productivity.

What makes SimScale particularly appealing to me isn't simply its appearance. It's the way the interface organizes complex engineering tasks into understandable workflows, maintains a clear visual hierarchy, and makes advanced functionality approachable without sacrificing technical depth.

I believe FieldCraft has an opportunity to go beyond matching the capabilities or interfaces of existing commercial software. It could help establish a new standard for how engineering simulation applications should look, feel, and function.

A genuinely modern multiphysics application could appeal not only to students and hobbyists but also to professional engineers who are accustomed to powerful software with outdated user experiences.

Since FieldCraft is still relatively early in its development, I think this could be an excellent opportunity to explore a more distinctive design direction.

I completely understand that the maintainers may have different priorities or a different vision for the project. I'm proposing this as a long-term design discussion, not an expectation or demand for an immediate redesign.

### Expected behaviour

Rather than simply refreshing icons or changing colors, I'd love to see FieldCraft explore a more comprehensive, workflow-first user interface.

Some ideas worth considering:

**1. Modern visual design**
- A clean, cohesive design language with consistent typography, spacing, and visual hierarchy.
- Carefully designed light and dark themes.
- Less visual clutter, with greater emphasis on simulation geometry and results.
- Contextual controls that appear when relevant rather than displaying every available operation simultaneously.
- Modern, responsive panels and dialogs.

**2. Guided simulation workflows**
- An intuitive process for creating a simulation, selecting physics, assigning materials, generating meshes, configuring boundary conditions, solving, and reviewing results.
- Clear visual indicators showing which setup stages are complete, incomplete, or contain errors.
- Progressive disclosure of advanced settings so beginners aren't immediately overwhelmed.
- Sensible defaults, while preserving access to advanced controls.

**3. More interactive 3D visualization**
- A large, central viewport that remains the focus of the application.
- Direct interaction with geometry, faces, boundaries, materials, and loads.
- Context-sensitive property panels linked to selections in the viewport.
- Smooth transitions between geometry, mesh, and simulation results.
- Clear, polished visualization of stress, deformation, pressure, temperature, and other physical quantities.

**4. Unified simulation management**
- A visually organized project dashboard.
- Easy comparison between different simulations and configurations.
- Clear simulation progress, convergence monitoring, and solver diagnostics.
- Convenient access to previous results without navigating through numerous technical menus.

**Closing thoughts**

I'm not suggesting that FieldCraft should copy SimScale's proprietary interface. Rather, I think SimScale provides an excellent example of the level of visual polish, accessibility, and workflow clarity that modern engineering applications can achieve.

It would be great to see FieldCraft explore its own distinctive interpretation of these principles.

Even a design exploration, community discussion, or a few alternative UI mockups could be valuable.

**Would the maintainers be open to considering a more substantial UI/UX redesign inspired by modern simulation platforms as a longer-term goal?**

Thank you for your work on FieldCraft and for making such an ambitious project open source!

### Pictures

_No response_

### References

[FieldCraft's existing roadmap](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/ROADMAP.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — acknowledgement of current UI/UX development.

title: Feature Request: Official Docker Image with Browser-Accessible GUI

### Current behaviour

FieldCraft currently provides desktop applications and other distribution methods, but I could not find an official Docker image that allows users to access its GUI through a web browser.

I currently use SolidCraft through Docker Compose, which allows users to access the application through a web browser without installing the desktop application on each PC.

I would like to use FieldCraft in the same way as SolidCraft: running it in a Docker container and accessing its GUI through a web browser.

- **Simplified deployment:** Users can access FieldCraft through a web browser without installing the application on each PC.

- **Consistent environments:** All users can work with the same application version and runtime environment.

Based on my experience with SolidCraft, I believe this would make FieldCraft much easier to deploy, maintain, and share within a community or organization.

Ideally, I would like to see:

- An official Docker image that includes the FieldCraft GUI.
- The ability to access and operate the GUI through a web browser.

FDM parts: take the layer direction from SolidCraft's print face, and report the stress across the layers
body:
### What are you trying to do

I check 3D-printed (FDM) parts. Their weak direction is across the layers: the tensile strength between layers is often a third to a half of the in-plane value. Today I set this up by hand for every part:
- an orthotropic material with its axis along the build direction;
- a results probe of σ_zz in that frame;
- a note of which way the part prints.

SolidCraft 0.28.0 now stores the face a body prints on (Print face, #8433). So the build direction is already in the design FieldCraft opens.

### How I imagine it working

- **Read the print face.** When a body in the opened design has a print face, FieldCraft offers it as that body's **build direction**: the outward normal of the print face, pointing into the bed. `inspect_model` lists it per body.
- **Material orientation from it:** `model.material.orientation {body, from: "print_face"}` (or a `build_direction` vector). An orthotropic material then puts its third axis along the build direction, with no manual frame.
- **FDM presets** (optional): a few named starting points, such as "PLA, PETG, ASA, PET-CF, 100 % infill, layer-direction factor k". These are clearly marked as rough values to replace with coupon data.
- **Results:** `show_results {field: "stress_across_layers"}`, which is the normal stress along the build direction, with its tension-only peak. A check, "across-layer tension ≤ allowable", gives a pass or fail and its margin.
- **Without a print face**, nothing changes. The user can still give `build_direction` directly.

### Why

It turns the most common printed-part failure check into one step, and it uses data SolidCraft now saves anyway. It also catches the classic mistake of printing a part on the wrong face: rotate the print face and re-run.

### Notes

The existing orthotropic elastic materials and the result frames cover the solver side. This is mostly orientation plumbing, a result field and a check.

title: Translate the desktop app's interface, starting with French
body:
### Current behaviour

The interface is English-only. Every label is an English string in the code: about 1,000 in `crates/ui-egui` (menus, panels, buttons, tooltips, status messages), plus the 170 command labels and the form fields' labels, hints and help in `crates/engine` (`CommandSpec.label`, `schema::Field`, the ribbon catalogue). There is no message catalogue and no language setting, so an engineer can't use FieldCraft in their own language.

### What you need and why

Many engineers, students and teaching labs in France, Belgium, Switzerland, Quebec and French-speaking Africa work in French. A pre-processor is full of domain terms (sets, sections, steps, loads, boundary conditions, result quantities), and a translated interface makes FieldCraft much easier to teach and adopt there. SolidCraft already ships a French interface, so a part opened from SolidCraft lands today in a FieldCraft that only speaks English. #734 also asks for documentation "available in the languages required for its intended markets"; this issue covers the app's interface only.

I'd like to do this work myself. Because it touches most of `ui-egui`, I'd rather agree on the approach with you before writing any code.

### Expected behaviour

- A **Language** preference (`files::Prefs`): `system` by default (the OS locale on desktop, `navigator.languages` on the web), or a language chosen from the list. Untranslated messages fall back to English.
- **Only what's shown is translated.** Command ids, parameter keys, JSON replies, CLI output, the MCP tools, control-channel replies, file formats, unit symbols and user names stay exactly as they are, so scripts, agents and decks never depend on the UI language. Tests and scenarios always run in English, so they read the same text on every machine.
- **Guarded coverage**, as SolidCraft does: tests fail when a command label, ribbon tab/panel or menu label is missing from the English catalogue, and a report lists what each language is still missing.
- **An original French catalogue** with a short glossary for translators. Some French words cover several English ones: *contrainte* is both *stress* and *constraint*, *pas* can be a time increment or a step, *étape* is an analysis step, and *chargement* a load or a loading history. Each meaning needs its own entry and a note. No wording is taken from commercial CAE products' localised interfaces; the translation is written from FieldCraft's English text.

Suggested slicing, each part its own PR and each commit building and passing its tests:
1. The catalogue mechanism, the language preference, system-locale matching and the coverage tests, with English alone (no visible change).
2. The `ui-egui` texts and the engine's display labels go through the catalogue (still no visible change in English).
3. `fr.json`, the glossary, and before/after screenshots.

### Questions for the maintainer

1. **Which mechanism?** There are two candidates in the Craft family:
   - SolidCraft's `crates/ui-egui/src/i18n.rs`: per-app JSON catalogues in `assets/locales/`, keyed by stable ids plus an adapter from engine labels, and documented in `docs/localization.md`. It would be adapted under MIT OR Apache-2.0 and noted in ATTRIBUTION.md.
   - The shared `craft-i18n` crate in `storytold/craft-libs`: shared and per-app catalogues, plurals, number formatting, system locale. FieldCraft already depends on craft-libs, but at a revision that predates this crate, so the pin would move and it brings ICU4X dependencies (licence and wasm checks via `deny.toml`/`cargo xtask wasm`).
2. **Engine labels:** translate them in the UI from `cmd.<command id>` keys, which leaves `CommandSpec` untouched (my preference), or change the engine's types?
3. **Scope:** French alone at first, with the mechanism open to other languages later?

### Pictures

Screenshots of the ribbon, a command form and the results panel in French will be in the last PR.

### References

- SolidCraft `docs/localization.md` and `crates/ui-egui/src/i18n.rs` (tangency-labs/solidcraft)
- `storytold/craft-libs` `crates/i18n/README.md`
- Unicode CLDR language matching (BCP 47 tags, fallback from a region to its base language)

title: lbm-gpu: the throughput benchmarks fail in parallel on NVIDIA with "the readback did not complete"
body:
### Observed failure

The `lbm-gpu` throughput benchmarks (`crates/lbm-gpu/tests/throughput.rs`, all `#[ignore]`d, so part of `cargo xtask test --heavy`) fail now and then on a real NVIDIA card when they run in parallel, the default for `cargo test`:

```
thread 'smagorinsky_cost' panicked at crates/lbm-gpu/tests/throughput.rs:312:40:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: Backend("GPU: the readback did not complete")
thread 'cell_updates_per_second' panicked at crates/lbm-gpu/tests/throughput.rs:121:28:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: Backend("GPU: the readback did not complete")
```

`zone_throughput_and_diagnostic_cost` failed once as well (at `throughput.rs:54`, `device.advance(32).unwrap()`).

### Reproduction

```
FIELDCRAFT_GPU=hardware FIELDCRAFT_REQUIRE_GPU=1 \
  cargo test --profile ci -p fieldcraft-lbm-gpu --test throughput -- --include-ignored
```

Repeated on the same machine, `develop` at cb97611:

| | runs | failed with "the readback did not complete" |
|---|---|---|
| default test threads | 12 | 4 (1–2 tests each); one more run ended without any test result, its output was not kept |
| `--test-threads=1` | 1 | 0 |
| `smagorinsky_cost` alone | 2 | 0 |

### Evidence

No Xid in the guest's kernel log, no PCIe/AER messages on the host, the card idle at 41 °C afterwards. `verification.rs` and the other tests of the crate pass in the same runs.

### Expected behaviour

The benchmarks pass, as they do one at a time. CI runs them on lavapipe only, so it does not see this.

### Investigation

`verification.rs` takes a shared turn (`static TURN: Mutex<()>`, #616) since the parallel hang in #614 (NVIDIA, concurrent devices); `throughput.rs` does not, so its six benchmarks share the card. The error comes from `read` in `crates/lbm-gpu/src/native.rs`: `device.poll(PollType::Wait { .. })` returns `Ok`, but the `map_async` callback has not run yet, so `rx.try_recv()` is empty. The runs end in about 60 s, well inside `DEVICE_TIMEOUT` (120 s). I have not looked further into why the poll returns before the callback. Taking the same turn in `throughput.rs` would also keep the measured rates clean (in parallel they read 837 M cell updates/s against 1115–1686 M/s alone).

### Version and platform

`develop` at cb97611 (0.7.0). NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Ti, NVIDIA open kernel module 615.78.08, Vulkan, power-limited to 186 W, passed through to a Fedora 44 x86_64 KVM guest (kernel 7.2.14).

title: fieldcraft-cli panics when its stdout is closed (| head) or full
body:
### Observed failure

`fieldcraft-cli` panics when the reader of its stdout goes away early:

```
$ fieldcraft-cli commands | head -1
…first line…
thread 'main' panicked at library/std/src/io/stdio.rs:1168:9:
failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe (os error 32)
```

Exit status 101. The same happens for every subcommand that writes to stdout (`--help`, `--version`, `features`, `crashes`, `commands`, …). A full stdout panics the same way: `fieldcraft-cli --version > /dev/full` → `failed printing to stdout: No space left on device (os error 28)`, exit 101.

### Reproduction

1. Build `fieldcraft-cli` from `develop` (cb97611).
2. `fieldcraft-cli commands | head -1; echo "${PIPESTATUS[0]}"` prints `101` after the panic.
3. `fieldcraft-cli --version > /dev/full; echo $?` prints `101` after the panic.

### Evidence

The panic text above, from both runs. No crash report is written: it is the CLI, not the app.

### Expected behaviour

AGENTS.md, "Never crash". A reader that stops early (`| head`, `| grep -m1`) is a normal way to use a command-line tool: the output should just end, exit 0. A write that fails for another reason (a full disk) means the output is incomplete: report it (`error: writing to stdout: …`) and exit non-zero, without a panic.

### Investigation

Rust ignores SIGPIPE, so a write to a closed pipe returns `EPIPE`, and `println!` panics on any write error. All of the CLI's stdout goes through `println!`/`print!` in `apps/fieldcraft-cli/src`.

### Version and platform

`develop` at cb97611 (0.7.0), Fedora 44 x86_64.

---

I have a fix for this, with a regression test, verified locally: the CLI's own `println!`/`print!` (shadowing std's in `apps/fieldcraft-cli`) end the output quietly when the reader is gone, and report any other write error from `main` as a failed command. May I open a pull request?

title: Staircase geometry: drag depends on how many cells span the body and on where it sits on the grid (periodic Stokes sphere +11.7 % at R = 3 cells; Schäfer–Turek C_d,max +6.7 % at D/Δx 20 and −8.5 % on a half-cell shift)
body:
Part of the LES accuracy and stability tracking issue (#785). ## Observed Obstacles are voxelised (a cell is solid when its centre is inside the body) and bounded by halfway bounce-back, so a curved body is a staircase of lattice faces. Two steady or laminar controls on develop `cb976117` quantify what that costs in drag, independently of any turbulence model: **Periodic array of Stokes spheres** (theory: Hasimoto 1959 with Sangani & Acrivos 1982's higher terms, K = 2.0215 at volume fraction 0.0276): | Sphere radius | Box | K measured | vs theory | |---|---|---|---| | 3 cells | 16³ | 2.2572 | **+11.66 %** | | 6 cells | 32³ | 2.0550 | +1.66 % | Mass is conserved to roundoff and the wall force equals the driving force at steady state in both, so the error is geometric, not a force-accounting error. **Confined cylinder, Schäfer & Turek Re 100 (2D-2Z, scaled to D = 1), TRT, lattice velocity 0.05:** | Grid / change | Mean C_d ± 95 % half-width | C_d,max | vs 3.22–3.24 | St (ref. 0.295–0.305) | Outcome | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | D/Δx = 20, τ 0.52, CPU | 3.34682 ± 0.00031 | 3.44664 | **+6.7 %** | 0.29870 (periods 0.29837–0.29891) | stable 120 D/U | | Same, GPU f32 | 3.346814 ± 0.000306 | 3.44659 | +6.7 % | 0.298703 | CPU/GPU C_d differ by 7 × 10⁻⁵ % | | D/Δx = 20, regularized | 3.37737 ± 0.00046 | 3.49203 | +8.1 % | 0.29746 | collision changes C_d by +0.9 % | | D/Δx = 20, body shifted +0.5 cell in y | 3.10202 ± 0.00039 | 3.15345 | **−2.4 %** | 0.30442 | mean −7.3 %, peak −8.5 % from unshifted | | D/Δx = 10, τ 0.51 | invalid | — | — | — | unstable at 91.4 D/U (CPU), 47.6 D/U (GPU): lattice speed 0.66 | A half-cell shift of the body moves the peak drag by 8.5 % at 20 cells per diameter. (The shift also moves the body 0.025 D in the 4.1 D channel, so it is a combined placement sensitivity, not a pure grid-phase error; the solver has no way to translate the grid under fixed physical boundaries.) For the LES cases the implication is that 12–24 cells per diameter (the resolutions the SGS τ floor admits at Re 3900) carry a geometric drag error of the same order as the terms being studied, and that the N = 8 quasi-2D runs with the body shifted half a cell (C_d 2.29 against 1.87 unshifted on the GPU, +22 %) cannot be read as a wall-placement effect at all because both drift by about 0.9 between window halves. body:
Part of the LES accuracy and stability tracking issue (#785). ## Observed The solver's automatic time step sets the characteristic lattice velocity to 0.05 (Ma 0.087), where the weakly compressible error is of order Ma² ≈ 0.75 %. title: Short-window block error bars understate LES drag error: a later 400–600 D/U window raises the Re 3900 cylinder's C_d by 22.6 % while the force noise grows, and ±0.0003 intervals sit on a 6.7 % bias
body:
Part of the LES accuracy and stability tracking issue (#785). ## Observed The conditional 95 % half-width from eight block means describes sampling noise under stationarity. In the audited LES runs it misses three things that dominate the actual error: drift within the window, deterioration after the window, and the discretisation and model bias that no amount of averaging removes. **1. The late window is worse, not better.** The baseline Re 3900 cylinder (N = 12, HRR, GPU) was extended from 200 to 600 D/U; the force history repeats the original run bit for bit through 200 D/U, then its oscillations grow. | Window | Mean C_d ± 95 % half-width | Block lag-1 | C_d,max | C_l rms | ρ range at the end | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 100–200 D/U | 1.3539 ± 0.0401 | 0.619 | 8.3 | 0.32 | 0.954–1.050 | | 400–600 D/U | **1.6602 ± 0.0747 (+22.6 %)** | −0.599 | **24.4** | **1.36** | 0.882–1.143 | With a divergence-free analytic start (ψ = U y (1 − R²/r²)(1 − e^(−(r−R)/0.1D))), which removes 99.7 % of the rapid lift peak's power in the first window, the mean is unchanged (1.3585 ± 0.0542) but the run deteriorates the same way later: 400–600 D/U gives 1.4818 ± 0.0728 (+9.1 % on its own early mean), C_d,max 19.1, C_l rms 0.77 (five times its early value), with the dominant recorded lift peak at 4.31 U/D. Initialisation delays the growth; it does not remove it. Neither interval overlaps the experimental 0.99 ± 0.05. **2. Drift inside the window.** The CPU quasi-2D N = 8 HRR case (roundoff-seeded, late symmetry breaking) reports 1.187 ± 0.455 with the second-half mean 0.863 above the first-half mean, i.e. 73 % of the mean: an interval of ±0.455 on a series whose blocks rise from about 0.75 to 1.89. With an explicit planar seed the same case gives 1.870 ± 0.030 with drift −0.008. The "height 18 D" CPU variant reports 0.976 ± 0.415, which happens to bracket the experiment, with a drift of 0.615 (blocks from 0.65 to 1.83); that agreement is accidental. **3. A narrow interval on a biased mean.** The laminar Schäfer–Turek Re 100 control (N = 20, TRT) reports mean C_d 3.34682 ± 0.00031 and C_d,max 3.44664, which is +6.7 % against the benchmark's 3.22–3.24. The interval is a hundredth of a percent; the error is 6.7 %, from the grid and boundary placement (a half-cell body shift moves it by −8.5 %, see GEOMETRY). **4. Zero-crossing Strouhal numbers.** Counting upward crossings of the mean-subtracted lift gives St 2.9 for the 3D cylinder (reference 0.215), 2.1 for the square (0.132) and 0.74 for the steady sphere (none), because the recorded force carries rapid oscillations. title: Musker wall model: the carried wall stress is 16.75 % below Dean while the model's inferred stress is within 2 % (channel Re_τ 950)
body:
Part of the LES accuracy and stability tracking issue (#785).

## Observed

The Malaspinas & Sagaut reproduction at Re_τ 950, N = 10 cells per δ, rerun on develop `cb976117`:

| Quantity | Value | Against Dean (1978) |
|---|---|---|
| C_f from the wall model's inferred u_τ | 0.0053667 | **+2.00 %** |
| C_f from the drag the flow carries (the body force that holds the bulk velocity) | 0.0043803 | **−16.75 %** |
| requested wall stress ⟨u_τ²⟩ / carried wall stress (mean force) | 1.03713 / 0.83318 | ratio 1.245 |
| mean model u_τ / carried u_τ | 1.0103 / 0.9128 | +10.7 % |

The sampling uncertainty of the carried force is 0.83318 ± 0.00687 (95 %, 25 blocks of 2 δ/u_τ, lag-1 block correlation 0.03), i.e. a C_f half-width of about 0.82 %. It cannot account for a 16.75 % deficit.

The velocity profile scaled by the carried u_τ lies above the DNS at every point (U⁺ +7.6 % to +12.1 % against Lee & Moser, +8.0 % at y⁺ 43 up to +12.1 % at y⁺ 304).

This is the same discrepancy the manual records (`docs/manual/fluid/les.md`, "The drag the flow carries": −16.8 / −13.7 / −14.1 % at N = 10 / 20 / 30), reproduced independently. The existing test passes because its acceptance criteria are the model-inferred C_f and the paper's profile error E; the carried drag is reported but not gated.

The momentum budget is **not** the cause: the per-step balance of the Musker momentum-budget test closes to 2–3 × 10⁻¹⁴ of the total population momentum (TRT, RR and MRT), and the reconstruction impulse is included in the reported force. The gap is between the stress the model infers at x₂ and the stress the rebuilt cell plus its bounce-back links actually transmit.

## Reproduce (from develop)

The existing study, on a GPU (the audit used an NVIDIA GB10, Vulkan, f32, in-place streaming):

```sh
FIELDCRAFT_PAPER_CHANNEL=950:10 cargo test --release -p fieldcraft-lbm-gpu --test verification \
  study_malaspinas_and_sagaut_s_channel_against_lee_and_moser -- --ignored --nocapture
```

What that study sets up (all from `paper_channel` in `crates/lbm-gpu/tests/verification.rs`):

| Item | Setting |
|---|---|
| Domain | periodic channel, δ = 1, 2πδ × 2δ × 2πδ rounded to whole cells; x and z periodic, y_min and y_max no-slip walls (halfway bounce-back) |
| Grid | N = 10 cells per δ (Δx = 0.1), 79 380 cells; first cell centre at y⁺ ≈ 43, matching point y⁺ ≈ 130 |
| Fluid | ρ = 1, ν = 1 / 950 |
| Collision | `"mrt"` (d'Humières et al. 2002 rates: 1.19, 1.4, 1.2, 1.98; the five stresses at 1/(3(ν + ν_t) + ½)) |
| Turbulence | `{"type": "smagorinsky", "constant": 0.08, "wall_model": "musker"}` |
| Forcing | body force along x, updated every step to hold the bulk velocity at Dean's correlation for Re_τ 950 (Re_m 37 042), their eq. 67 |
| Lattice velocity | u_m = 0.1 (Δt = 0.1 Δx / U_m) |
| Start | the perturbed profile in the test (1.15 U_m (1 − |η|⁸) plus sinusoidal perturbations) |
| Averaging | from 20 δ/u_τ, at least 50 δ/u_τ, stop when the wall force's 95 % half-width is below 1 % with decorrelated 2 δ/u_τ blocks; end at 150 δ/u_τ. This run stopped at 70 δ/u_τ (136 479 steps, 93 s) |
| Reference | Dean's C_f at Re_m; Hoyas & Jiménez `Re950.prof` (the Re_τ 934 channel of del Álamo & Jiménez) and Lee & Moser's profile |

The log prints both C_f values, the requested / carried stress ratio and the profile table.

## Measured (this rerun)

```
force: 0.83318 ± 0.00687 (95 %, 25 blocks of 2 δ/u_τ, lag-1 correlation 0.03); C_f ± 0.82 %
stress at the wall: requested by the model ⟨u_τ²⟩ 1.03713, carried (mean force) 0.83318, ratio 1.2448
M&S comparison: ⟨u_τ⟩ model 1.0103, carried 0.9128 (gap +10.69 %); C_f model 0.00537 (+2.00 % of Dean 0.00526), carried 0.00438 (-16.75 %, -13.90 % of the DNS 0.00509); E 2.08 %
measured Re_τ 867, U_b⁺ 21.368 (LM 19.81), U_c⁺ 24.07 (LM 22.42)
```

## Notes on the reported error measure

- The paper's E (its eq. 69, `100/M · sqrt(Σ relative error²)`) is 2.08 % here with M = 20 (the folded ten-point profile counted on both halves). The ordinary RMS relative error over the same points is E·√M ≈ 9.3 %. E shrinks with the point count, so it is not a resolution-independent percentage.
- The "Re950" profile in the repository is Torroja's `Re950.prof`, i.e. the Re_τ 934 channel; the separate Lee & Moser "950" profile is an interpolation between their 550 and 1000 cases. Both conventions were kept here.

## What this issue does not claim

- It does not claim the GPU is at fault: the CPU/GPU momentum budgets close, and the manual's N = 10/20/30 series shows the same gap on every grid.
- It does not claim the inferred C_f is right and the carried one wrong, or the reverse; only that the two differ by 16.75 % and that `solve.fluid` reports the carried one.
- The manual's Re_τ 1000 and 2000 rows (−9 to −15 % except Re_τ 2000 at N = 30) were not rerun in this audit.

References: Malaspinas & Sagaut (2014), J. Comput. Phys. 275:25–40, doi:10.1016/j.jcp.2014.06.020. Dean (1978), J. Fluids Eng. 100(2):215–223, doi:10.1115/1.3448633. Lee & Moser (2015), J. Fluid Mech. 774:395–415, doi:10.1017/jfm.2015.268. Hoyas & Jiménez (2008), Phys. Fluids 20:101511, doi:10.1063/1.3005862.

title: LES accuracy and stability: drag and wall-stress errors (tracking)
body:
## Symptom

@jyviko reported that large-eddy simulation in FieldCraft "doesn't work reliably", with drag discrepancies of 15–40 % against references, and pointed at `docs/manual/fluid/les.md`, whose own record shows no wall model passing the drag gate. This issue tracks the specific errors and gaps behind that, each as a sub-issue with a self-contained reproduction and its measured numbers. No fixes are proposed here; the sub-issues record what is wrong and how to see it.

**Baseline:** develop `cb976117889edf8de5f093ba949980b0aa79c1e2`, production solver untouched. GPU runs on an NVIDIA GB10 (Vulkan, f32, in-place streaming); CPU runs in f64.

**What was measured:** 62 case records (47 completed, 13 stopped as unstable, 2 refused at setup) across the Malaspinas & Sagaut channel at Re_τ 950, a laminar confined-cylinder control (Schäfer & Turek Re 100), a 3D circular cylinder at Re 3900 (three resolutions and a one-factor sweep of twenty variants), a square cylinder at Re 22 000, a sphere at Re 100, quasi-2D Re 3900 probes on both backends, the periodic Stokes sphere array, the 80-case wall-stability sweep, and force-budget checks. "Completed" below is an execution status, not a validation verdict.

## Sub-issues

| # | Error or gap | Headline |
|---|---|---|
| #786 | Musker wall model: carried wall stress ≠ inferred stress | channel Re_τ 950, N = 10: inferred C_f **+2.0 %**, carried C_f **−16.75 %** vs Dean; requested/carried stress 1.245 |
| #787 | 3D cylinder at Re 3900 overpredicts drag and does not converge | C_d **1.354 ± 0.040 (+36.8 %)** vs 0.99; N = 12/16/24 give 1.354 / 1.323 / 1.338 |
| #788 | Cylinder drag sensitivity to setup | one-cell span **+33 %**, Musker on **+80 %**, dynamic HRR σ **+22 %** (and spanwise energy ÷200); C_s, Mach, domain, outlet each within ±3 % |
| #789 | Square cylinder at Re 22 000 | C_d **4.11 ± 0.14 vs ≈ 2.1 (+95 %)**, C_d,max 24.8, crossing St 2.1 vs 0.132 |
| #790 | MRT fails almost at once at the LES bluff-body settings | 3D cylinder by step 120 (0.5 D/U), square by step 128, quasi-2D by step 599 (CPU) / 816 (GPU) |
| #791 | Coarse TRT completes with negative mean drag | quasi-2D N = 8: C_d **−3.84 ± 4.53** (CPU), −2.08 ± 5.55 (GPU); guard never trips |
| #792 | Re 100 sphere with TRT goes unstable at the inlet | GPU at 11.4 D/U, CPU at 19.7 D/U, first invalid cells at x = 0; regularized survives at C_d **+12.5 %** with spurious unsteadiness |
| #793 | Runtime guard certifies execution, not validity | completed runs with ρ 0.72–1.37, local Ma 0.35, C_d,max 20× the mean |
| #794 | `spalding_bounce_halfway` grows a wall-row checkerboard | +5.6e-5 to +1.3e-1 per step, every collision, every τ̄; on-node form damps it |
| #795 | Channel study stop rule tests signed lag-1 | alternating blocks (lag-1 ≈ −0.95) pass as decorrelated; measured LES lag-1 down to −0.83 |
| #796 | Short-window block error bars understate the error | 400–600 D/U window raises C_d **+22.6 %** while C_d,max goes 8 → 24; ±0.0003 interval on a +6.7 % bias |
| #797 | Compressibility at the default lattice velocity 0.05 | ρ ±5 %, local Ma 0.15 at Re 3900; halving it gives ±0.4 % but C_d stays +38.6 % |
| #798 | Staircase geometry resolution and placement | Stokes sphere **+11.7 %** at R = 3 cells (+1.7 % at 6); Schäfer–Turek C_d,max +6.7 % at D/Δx 20, −8.5 % on a half-cell shift |

The first three carry the 15–40 % class of error on their own; the rest either invalidate "completed" runs or hide the first three.

## Checked and found consistent (no need to re-check)

- **Smagorinsky term and lattice scaling.** τ_eff = (τ₀ + √(τ₀² + 18√2 C_s² ‖P‖/ρ)) / 2 with the off-diagonal entries counted twice, P including the half-force term, Δ = Δx; the simple-shear unit test gives ν₀ + C² γ. No factor-of-two error. (`crates/lbm/src/turbulence.rs`)
- **Static-body Galilean terms.** The momentum exchange has no moving-surface relative-velocity term; for the stationary bodies here that term is identically zero, so it cannot change any drag in this audit.
- **Force budgets close.** The Musker channel momentum budget closes per step to 2–3 × 10⁻¹⁴ of the total population momentum (TRT, RR, MRT), reconstruction impulse included. An independent population-momentum balance around a periodic cylinder agrees with the link momentum exchange to 7 × 10⁻¹² (lattice force) under HRR at τ = 0.52 and 0.5005, with the SGS model on. The Stokes sphere array's wall force equals its driving force and conserves mass to roundoff. The rapid force oscillations at high Re exist while the discrete momentum accounting is correct.
- **CPU vs GPU.** On the laminar Schäfer–Turek control the mean C_d differs by 7 × 10⁻⁵ % and St by 4 × 10⁻⁴ %; on the regularized variant by 9 × 10⁻⁴ %. On the explicitly seeded quasi-2D Re 3900 case the two backends agree to 0.03 %. f32 is not the cause of the drag errors. (CPU and GPU do break symmetry at different times from a roundoff-only seed, and fail at different steps when a case is unstable; that is precision sensitivity of the onset, not a result difference.)
- **Mach alone.** Halving the lattice velocity removes the density excursion and leaves the Re 3900 drag excess (#797).
- **Force sampling cadence.** Four-times denser sampling and an odd stride give the same mean within 0.1 % and the same spectral peak.
- **Domain and outlet.** Height 18 D, length 36 D and a uniform outlet move the Re 3900 short-window mean by at most 2.5 %.
- **The ordinary test suites pass** on the baseline: `fieldcraft-lbm` 180 passed / 27 ignored, `fieldcraft-lbm-gpu` 62 passed / 15 ignored on the GB10, clippy clean. They establish local consistency, not turbulent drag accuracy.

## Caveats

- @jyviko's own failing case (geometry, Re, wall model, reference) was not available, so none of the reproduced discrepancies can be identified as that case. They are independently built cases that land in the reported 15–40 % range (and beyond it for the square).
- Every bluff-body case here is deliberately coarse (8–24 cells per diameter), because that is what the SGS relaxation-time floor admits at these Reynolds numbers on grids that run in minutes; none is claimed converged. The channel case is the paper's own setup.
- Statistical intervals are conditional on stationarity and decorrelated blocks and exclude grid, domain and model error; the sub-issues report lag-1 correlation and half-window drift beside them for that reason.
- The manual's Han, Ooka & Kikumoto channel results (+53 % on MRT, −52 to −55 % on the hybrid collision at A20) and the Re_τ 1000 / 2000 Musker rows were not rerun; they are already recorded in `docs/manual/fluid/les.md`.

Related: #664 (CPU LES), #665 (GPU LES), #663, #557.

title: Proposal: engineer-facing technical documentation as part of feature acceptance
body:
﻿FieldCraft already requires cited numerical methods and reproducible verification tests. However, mathematical explanations are scattered across developer-oriented documents and Rust source comments.

**Proposal:** make documentation intended for engineers, not Rust developers, part of the **definition of done** for each new or significantly changed analysis capability declared ready for use.

A concise, versioned technical reference should cover:

1. **Theory:** physical assumptions, governing equations, defined notation, reasons for the chosen formulation, applicability and limitations.
2. **Verification:** links to reproducible oracle cases, published references, convergence checks and known failures.
3. **User guidance:** inputs, units, a worked example and interpretation of results.
4. **Publication and languages:** documentation delivered with the corresponding release, prepared for translation and available in the languages required for its intended markets.

Ideally, implementation, verification and source-language user documentation should be reviewed in the **same PR**. Experimental features can remain explicitly labelled as such.

A lightweight, reusable template/checklist would be a practical first step; there is no need to rewrite the existing documentation.

**Principle:** an engineer must be able to understand and assess a numerical method **without knowing or reading Rust**.

title: Fluid: walls where the surface is (interpolated bounce-back) for curved obstacles
body:
### Current behaviour

The lattice puts every obstacle wall half way between a fluid cell and a solid one, so a curved
wall is a staircase. On Schäfer & Turek's 2D-1 cylinder that costs about 1.3 % of drag on 20 cells
across it, and in a Poiseuille pipe it is the error that dominates (L2 4.5e-2 at 4 cells per radius,
9.5e-3 at 16).

### What you need and why

Drag and pressure drop on curved parts (cylinders, ducts, fins) within about 1 % of the
reference without very fine grids.

### Expected behaviour

An option on the fluid domain, `walls: halfway | interpolated | quadratic` (default `halfway`, so
nothing changes unless asked), that puts each wall link's bounce-back where the obstacle's surface
really crosses it, linear and quadratic (Bouzidi, Firdaouss & Lallemand 2001). The crossing comes
from the obstacle's triangle tree (a segment–triangle test, Möller & Trumbore 1997). CPU and GPU
(the GPU runs the linear one). Heat keeps its walls half way (the curved conducting interfaces are
#631).

Two findings from trying it, in case they matter elsewhere:

- `schafer_turek_2d1_cylinder_drag_and_lift` runs 10 time units, about one viscous time D²/ν at the
  cylinder. The wake is still settling then, and the drag reads several percent high for every wall
  and collision. At 40 units the half-way TRT cylinder on 20 cells is c_D 5.655 (+1.3 %) instead of
  5.773 (+3.4 %), and Δp (extrapolated to the surface) is inside the interval.
- An interpolation's cells behind a link have to wrap across periodic faces; otherwise a case one
  cell deep takes half its links half way.

Measured on a working branch (settled 2D-1, 20 cells across the cylinder):

| Case | Half-way | Interpolated | Quadratic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Poiseuille pipe, L2, 4 cells/radius | 4.5e-2 | 6.6e-3 | 3.4e-3 |
| Poiseuille pipe, L2, 16 cells/radius | 9.5e-3 | 6.5e-4 | 7.7e-4 |
| 2D-1 c_D (ref 5.57–5.59) | 5.655 (+1.34 %) | 5.610 (+0.54 %) | 5.598 (+0.32 %) |
| 2D-1 Δp (ref 0.1172–0.1176) | 0.1172 | 0.1168 (−0.5 %) | 0.1163 (−0.9 %) |

GPU checked on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Laptop GPU (Windows, DX12/Vulkan via wgpu): the
interpolated sphere matches the CPU to 3.4e-6 in velocity and 2.4e-6 in drag.

I'd like to take this one, with a PR against `develop`.

### References

- M. Bouzidi, M. Firdaouss, P. Lallemand, *Momentum transfer of a Boltzmann-lattice fluid with
  boundaries*, Phys. Fluids 13, 3452 (2001).
- T. Möller, B. Trumbore, *Fast, minimum storage ray-triangle intersection*, J. Graphics Tools 2(1)
  (1997).
- M. Schäfer, S. Turek, *Benchmark computations of laminar flow around a cylinder* (1996).

title: Proposal: NAFEMS Test 51 and FV5 modal oracle benchmarks
body:
## Proposal from @flexcut

I would like to contribute **reproducible NAFEMS free-vibration verification cases** to `tests/oracle/`. The models were constructed and solved directly with **FieldCraft v0.7.0 on Windows** from published problem descriptions, without using or extracting inputs from any commercial CAE program.

I am opening this issue before proposing a PR, in accordance with `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

### NAFEMS Test 51 — deep simply-supported *solid* beam

Primary source consulted: *Selected Benchmarks for Natural Frequency Analysis* (NAFEMS, 1987), Test 51 (original printed benchmark sheet). Dimensions L=10 m, section 2×2 m, E=200 GPa, Poisson ratio 0.3, density 8000 kg/m³.

Boundary conditions in local coordinates: u_x′=u_z′=0 on edge AA′; u_z′=0 on edge BB′; u_y′=0 on side y′=2 m. Consistent mass matrix. The published discretizations were recreated using FieldCraft's `mesh.block`.

| Mode | NAFEMS f_r (Hz) | FieldCraft 5×1×1 HEX20 (Hz) | DIANA published HEX20 (Hz) | FieldCraft 10×1×3 HEX8 (Hz) | DIANA published HEX8 (Hz) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 38.200 | 38.268448 | 38.268 | 40.721333 | 40.721 |
| 2 | 85.210 | 87.659445 | 87.659 | 88.663649 | 88.663 |
| 3 | 152.230 | 157.492124 | 157.49 | 164.333322 | 164.33 |
| 4 | 245.530 | 259.003128 | 259.00 | 275.220148 | 275.22 |
| 5 | 297.050 | 306.010243 | 306.01 | 306.629679 | 306.63 |

Independent published source: [DIANA verification manual, NAFEMS free-vibration cases 51hx20 and 51hx8b](https://manuals.dianafea.com/d103/Verify/Verifyse6.html), tables 3.75 and 3.77.

**Critical qualification:** The original NAFEMS sheet distinguishes reference values `f_r` from discretization-specific test results `f_t`. The FieldCraft results reproduce the published DIANA frequencies for the two meshes, **not necessarily the NAFEMS continuum/reference frequencies**. Additional refinement (HEX20 10×2×2 and 20×3×3; HEX8 20×2×6 and 30×4×6) produced decreasing frequencies, some below `f_r`; this is an **open investigation**, not a proven solver bug or a reason to enlarge the tolerance. Further controls included rotating the entire model and its local boundary directions (frequencies unchanged to 6 decimal places) and comparing consistent/lumped mass and HEX8 incompatible-mode variants.

### NAFEMS Test 5 (FV5) — 1-D deep simply-supported beam

Same 10 m length, square 2×2 m section and material. `beam2` Timoshenko elements; consistent-mass mesh refinement (5, 10, 20, 40, 80 elements), plus a 5-element lumped-mass run. At 80 elements:

| Mode(s) | FieldCraft (Hz) | Published NAFEMS target (Hz) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1–2 bending | 42.645149 | 42.650 |
| 3 torsion | 71.197230 | 71.200 |
| 4 axial | 125.002008 | 125.000 |
| 5–6 bending | 148.159113 | 148.150 |
| 7 torsion | 213.619141 | 213.610 |
| 8–9 bending | 283.535920 | 283.470 |

Reference cross-check: [ANSYS/LS-DYNA verification manual, VM-LSDYNA-SOLVE-064](https://ansyshelp.ansys.com/public/views/secured/corp/v261/en/lsdyna_vm/vm-lsdyna-solve-064.html). Independent analytical checks were made for 125 Hz axial quarter-wave and the Saint-Venant torsional modes (~71.196 and ~213.588 Hz). The original Test 5 sheet was unavailable in the hardcopy inspected, so this published secondary source would be cited explicitly.

### Contribution proposal

- Original FieldCraft `recipe.json`, a source-cited `expected.json` with justified tolerances, and a short README documenting geometry, BCs, element formulation, modal ordering, convergence evidence and limitations.
- Produce `fixture.json` using `cargo xtask oracle --case` and `--bless` **only after** a passing test, and regenerate `docs/oracle.md`.
- No copying of NAFEMS/vendor page images, model decks, text or commercial software outputs. Only published numerical target values with attribution.
- Keep mesh-specific regression verification separate from the unresolved continuum-reference investigation.

Would the maintainers welcome these cases? In particular, would you prefer separate HEX8/HEX20 oracle directories for Test 51, and FV5 in a subsequent PR?

— @flexcut

title: 0.7.5: reproducible heat-exchanger tutorials and release videos
body:
## Goal
The maintainer requests videos that help people use 0.7.5 to model flow and heat transfer in a heat exchanger. Deliver tutorials from reproducible release samples, not only a promotional animation.

## Proposed series
- [ ] **Your first heat exchanger (8–12 min):** geometry and fluid passages, materials, conducting wall, inlet/outlet and fan/pump or prescribed-flow assumptions, resolution, resource estimate, solve and save. Start from a supplied model/recipe.
- [ ] **Where does the heat go? (3–5 min):** velocity/temperature sections and streamlines, both outlet temperatures, heat duty, pressure loss and mass/energy budgets from the same solved model.
- [ ] **Choose a fan and compare fin spacing (5–8 min):** one controlled design change, fan/system operating point, cooling benefit versus pressure drop, and comparable convergence/resolution.
- [ ] **Can you trust this result? (about 5 min):** validation reference, refinement, convergence of running means for LES, uncertainty and model limits.

## Definition of done
- Inputs/recipes, exact version/commit, solve settings, hardware/runtime and saved outputs accompany each video; a viewer can reproduce the result.
- Captions and legends show physical units and distinguish measured numerical results from assumptions.
- Air-side-only examples are labelled as such. A full exchanger tutorial requires demonstrated coupled coolant/air support.
- A physical transient is labelled with physical time; accelerated steady-state heat-capacity runs and iteration playback are never presented as physical warm-up.
- No use of commercial CAE assets or models; original SolidCraft geometry and the repository's capture workflow.
- Publish gallery links, a thumbnail/hero still and a short release clip only once the final results and commands match the release build.

Related tooling: `tools/cooling`, `tools/flow-clip`, and `docs/examples.md`. The existing `cooling-aio` airflow clip is a starting point, but its held-temperature/air-side assumptions must remain visible.

title: 0.7.5: specify and verify coupled air/coolant heat-exchanger domains
body:
## Goal for 0.7.5
Model flow and heat transfer in a heat exchanger with distinct hot/cold fluid passages and a conducting separator. The existing AIO sample solves only the air side with an assumed coolant temperature; neither a drawn tube nor two independent solves represents a coupled liquid-to-air exchanger.

## Source audit (develop 7d9c027d71)
- `FluidDomain` has one fluid `material` (`crates/model/src/fluids.rs`). Multiple domain definitions are allowed.
- `Setup::new` selects a single fluid step/domain; `solve_fluid_on` builds one `Flow` and runs its backend (`crates/lbm/src/setup.rs`, `solve.rs`).
- Conducting obstacles exchange heat with that domain's fluid. I found no orchestration that exchanges the wall state/flux between different fluid solves.
- CPU/GPU CHT (#609/#651) and thermal contact resistance (#677) therefore provide necessary pieces, but do not establish two-fluid coupling.

## Specify before implementation
- [ ] Choose the minimal supported exchanger: separate air/coolant circuits, fluid properties, geometry/wall thickness and prescribed flows or fan/pump conditions. Record whether the first accepted case is laminar or turbulent and why.
- [ ] Document domain ownership/occupancy, shared wall identity, conservative interface transfer, units, coupling iterations, under-relaxation, time stepping and stopping criteria. A shared wall's heat capacity/source must not be counted twice.
- [ ] Define support for steady vs transient runs and CPU/GPU combinations. Accelerated solid heat capacity may be used only with explicit steady-state semantics.
- [ ] Specify result/probe/export and save/reopen semantics for both circuits and the shared wall; reject unsupported combinations explicitly.

## Acceptance evidence
- [ ] A simple two-stream exchanger matches a cited analytical energy-balance/effectiveness reference at stated tolerances, with independently computed hot/cold heat duties and mass-flow-weighted outlet temperatures.
- [ ] Energy and mass budgets expose imbalance and external losses/sources, rather than hiding disagreement in a single reported duty.
- [ ] Spatial and coupling-tolerance refinement, pressure-drop checks, a closed/insulated energy test where applicable, and an existing single-domain regression suite.
- [ ] One reproducible cooling/exchanger model runs through the normal commands and UI and saves/reopens both sides' results. No hidden manual flux handoff.

The first deliverable is the coupling specification and a minimal reference case; implementation should be split into reviewable changes from that evidence. This is a single-phase two-fluid/domain workflow, not a request for multiphase/free-surface physics.

title: 0.7.5: split GPU population buffers beyond the per-buffer cell limit
body:
## Problem
The maintainer identified this as urgent for 0.7.5 in #642. The GPU currently allocates all 19 momentum populations in one storage buffer and rejects `4 * 19 * cells` above the device's per-buffer cap (`crates/lbm-gpu/src/native.rs`, `GpuFlow::with_options`). At a 2 GiB cap this is about 28 million cells, below the intended fine cooling grids even when total GPU memory is sufficient. #678 fixed overall solve caps, not this buffer layout limit.

## Scope
Split population storage into device-supported buffers while preserving the AA in-place and AB streaming paths, boundary handling, thermal/solid coupling and collision options. Choose the layout using actual device limits, checked arithmetic and a documented addressing scheme. Do not replace the limit with a larger fixed assumption.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Small grids match the existing layout (bit-for-bit when arithmetic order is unchanged; otherwise explain and justify the numerical tolerance) and CPU within existing tolerances, for both collisions and AA/AB, with and without heat/conducting solids.
- [ ] Test addressing and streaming across every buffer split, including boundary links; exercise a deliberately small test cap without allocating multi-GiB fixtures in normal CI.
- [ ] Include LES and fan/porous integration when those branches land; maintain device binding-limit checks.
- [ ] Memory estimates account for the actual buffer layout, staging, thermal fields, host state and requested output frames; impossible allocations fail before creating buffers and explain the limiting resource.
- [ ] Demonstrate a real-hardware case above the former per-buffer cell limit and report cells, memory, throughput and CPU-reference comparison on a smaller version.
- [ ] Preserve wasm builds and actionable errors for adapters that cannot support the layout.

Related: #642, #650, #678, #665. The maintainer offered this work to @bluecmd in #642; no implementation is claimed by filing this issue.

title: Epic: explicit dynamics for beams, shells and 2D structural elements
body:
### Current behaviour

FieldCraft's explicit solver supports one-point hex8 solids, nodal-pressure tet4 solids, and rod2/rod3 trusses, with formulation restrictions. Its element gate rejects beams, shells and general 2D continuum elements. Existing truss support does not provide beam bending or shell behaviour.

### What you need and why

Run transient structural analyses of slender members, thin-walled parts, and plane or axisymmetric sections with suitable structural elements. These models need bending, rotational inertia, thickness treatment or 2D kinematics that the current explicit element set does not provide.

### Expected behaviour

Extend explicit dynamics in separately reviewable element-family increments. Each increment must define its supported kinematics, materials, loads, constraints, contact and output, rather than assuming that every implicit capability transfers automatically.

Implementation work to split into linked child issues:

- [ ] **Beams:** translational and rotational dynamics, section stiffness and inertia, applied moments, and the chosen finite-rotation treatment.
- [ ] **Shells:** membrane and bending response, director/rotation updates, thickness integration and rotational inertia, with stabilization where the formulation needs it.
- [ ] **Plane continuum elements:** plane stress and plane strain, with an explicit support table for element orders and material formulations.
- [ ] **Axisymmetric continuum elements:** radial/axial kinematics, hoop terms, consistent mass and force integration, and treatment of nodes on the symmetry axis.

Shared acceptance criteria for each increment:

- [ ] Use a documented formulation derived from published literature; specify lumped mass/inertia and a justified stable time-step estimate.
- [ ] Verify rigid motion and the small-deformation limit. Finite-rotation or finite-strain support requires separate objectivity tests.
- [ ] Demonstrate mesh and time-step convergence against analytical or published structural benchmarks: beam vibration/bending, shell plate vibration or transient bending, plane wave propagation, and an axisymmetric radial response as appropriate.
- [ ] Report kinetic and internal energy, external work, and any stabilization or dissipative terms consistently. Check energy and momentum balances on applicable unloaded cases.
- [ ] Support the declared loads, boundary conditions and result fields through the existing command and result workflows.
- [ ] Document contact eligibility and mixed-element compatibility. Refuse unsupported combinations explicitly.
- [ ] Preserve the existing explicit solid and truss verification cases and deterministic CPU behaviour.

### References

- [Explicit solver element/formulation gate](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/crates/explicit/src/system.rs), `check_formulation`.
- [FieldCraft element families](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/elements.md).
- [FieldCraft roadmap](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/ROADMAP.md), explicit dynamics and shells milestones.

title: Nonlinear mechanics: finite-rotation reference-point couplings
body:
### Current behaviour

In nonlinear static analysis, FieldCraft's reference-point couplings retain the linear solver's small-rotation constraints and emit a warning. The surrounding solid can undergo finite deformation, but a coupled reference point cannot correctly impose a large rigid rotation on its attached region through those linear constraints.

### What you need and why

Apply loads and prescribed motion through a rotating fixture or end attachment. Examples include bending a flexible part through a large angle and rotating the loaded end of a deformable tube. A rigid rotation of the attachment should not introduce artificial deformation or stress into a region intended to move rigidly.

### Expected behaviour

Add finite-rotation kinematic reference-point couplings for nonlinear static steps, with a documented rotation representation and frame convention. Update the constraint equations and their consistent linearization as the configuration changes, and report reference-point reactions using the same convention.

Start with kinematic couplings. Finite-rotation distributing couplings should be specified separately because their load distribution and admissible deformation need their own treatment. Explicit-dynamics couplings are outside this request.

Acceptance criteria:

- [ ] A stress-free body driven through a finite rigid translation and rotation by a reference point preserves distances and develops no spurious strain or stress within a stated numerical tolerance.
- [ ] Rotation is supported about an arbitrary axis, including a sequence of rotations about different axes; document composition and prescribed-rotation semantics.
- [ ] In the small-rotation limit, results recover the existing linear coupling behaviour.
- [ ] A deforming cantilever or tube with a rotating end attachment passes a cited analytical or published benchmark with a mesh-convergence study.
- [ ] Reference-point forces and moments balance the corresponding nodal resultants in the documented configuration and frame.
- [ ] Check the linearization numerically and demonstrate nonlinear convergence on a smooth finite-rotation case; rejected increments restore the committed coupling state.
- [ ] Existing commands, saved models and results consistently express the new behaviour. Unsupported partial constraints or incompatible combinations are rejected explicitly.

### References

- [FieldCraft nonlinear mechanics documentation](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/fem.md): the Couplings paragraph documents the current small-rotation restriction.
- [FieldCraft element and degree-of-freedom framework](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/elements.md).

Select and cite the finite-rotation constraint formulation from published mechanics literature before implementation; each verification case should state its reference and tolerance.

title: Linear buckling: initial-stress stiffness for beams, shells and trusses
body:
### Current behaviour

FieldCraft's linear buckling solver builds initial-stress stiffness for solid and 2D continuum elements. It refuses beams, shells and trusses because their initial-stress stiffness is not implemented. Those structural element families are already available for linear static and frequency analysis.

### What you need and why

Assess the stability of beam frames, thin shell structures and prestressed pin-jointed assemblies using their structural meshes. A model that can be solved for its linear preload should be usable for an eigenvalue buckling analysis when its element formulations support that analysis.

### Expected behaviour

Extend the existing buckling procedure with formulation-consistent geometric stiffness for beams, shells and trusses, assembled from the preload state. Preserve the existing load-factor and mode-shape workflow, including mixed meshes where the supported elements share degrees of freedom.

For trusses, the feature is assembly stability and prestress effects: an axial-only truss does not acquire bending stiffness or represent the local flexural buckling of an individual member.

Contact-preloaded buckling needs a separate specification of the contact state and its linearization and is outside this request. Nonlinear postbuckling is also a separate procedure.

Acceptance criteria:

- [ ] Derive and document each element family's geometric stiffness from published theory, including its kinematic assumptions and supported preload states.
- [ ] Beam column critical loads and mode shapes converge to closed-form results for at least two end conditions; account for shear deformation where relevant.
- [ ] A simply supported shell plate under in-plane compression converges to its analytical buckling load and mode.
- [ ] A pin-jointed assembly reproduces an analytically derived prestress-dependent tangent or instability condition, without attributing bending resistance to truss members.
- [ ] Mixed supported-element models assemble consistently; rigid modes and insufficient constraints produce useful diagnostics.
- [ ] Existing solid and 2D buckling cases retain their documented accuracy. Each new reference case records mesh convergence and a justified tolerance.
- [ ] Document supported element/formulation combinations and make unsupported combinations fail by name.

### References

- [FieldCraft: linear buckling](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/fem.md#linear-buckling).
- [FieldCraft element families](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/elements.md).
- Follow-up to #87. Separate from the buckling result-type work in #174.

body: ### Current behaviour FieldCraft can mesh and solve a part's design space, but nothing tells you where the part needs its material. That is the classic minimum compliance problem: the stiffest layout of a static step within a volume limit. ### Expected behaviour I have this working on a branch rebased on develop (11 commits, not pushed yet), built while the tet mesher fixes in #687 were under way: tet-meshing parts for this work is where the folds of #666 turned up. title: Tet mesher: an exact swept-face check in place of the 30° boundary turn bound
body:
### Current behaviour
With the fixes for #666, a move of a boundary vertex in the tet quality stage (smoothing, ODT, the final snap) is refused when one of its boundary faces turns by more than 30° (`BOUNDARY_TURN_COS`, `turns_over`, the bound `collapse` already kept), or when one of its moved faces meets another boundary face in more than their shared vertices (the skin index). The 30° bound stands in for an intersection question:
- it is measured from where the vertex is when it moves, so successive passes can turn a face further;
- it is a floating-point threshold where the rest of the checks are exact;
- in a thin slot, where the interior angle at an edge is close to 360°, a fold needs less than 30°;
- the face-to-face skin test cannot see a fold across a shared edge: two triangles sharing an edge meet properly unless they lie in one plane on the same side.

### What you need and why
An exact check, depending only on the mesh, that no move or change folds the skin, including across an edge two boundary faces share.

### Expected behaviour
- A boundary vertex `v` moving from `x` to `p` sweeps, for each boundary face `(a, b, v)`, the tetrahedron `(a, b, x, p)`. A move is valid when each swept tetrahedron meets every other boundary face (not holding `v`) in their shared vertices alone, by an exact simplex test such as the facet recovery's `cdt::meet::meet_properly`, which already takes a tetrahedron and a triangle.
- `TetComplex::replace` does the same at each edge shared by a removed and a made boundary face: `(a, b, v_0, v_{m−1})` for an edge removal's 2-2 flip, `(p, q, a, b)` for a collapse, `(edge, old apex, new vertex)` for an insertion.
- The 30° bound then goes, or stays as a documented limit on how far a face may turn for shape fidelity, like `BOUNDARY_FLIP_COS`, not as the fold guard.

### References
- L. Diazzi, D. Panozzo, A. Vaxman, M. Attene, *Constrained Delaunay Tetrahedrization: A Robust and Practical Approach*, ACM TOG 42(6):181, 2023, §4.4: simplices meeting properly, as the facet recovery tests them.
- J. R. Shewchuk, *Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates*, DCG 18:305–363, 1997.

title: Lattice Boltzmann: Smagorinsky subgrid closure (LES) on the CPU
body:
**Why.** Without a turbulence model the lattice solver needs cell Reynolds numbers below roughly 30–40 (u·Δx/ν; the regularised collision at τ ≈ 0.508). Real cooling flows break that on any grid we can hold. The graphics card of #642 diverges with only 0.5 m/s into its intake on 0.5 mm cells: a jet in the 1.9 mm gap between the VRM blocks and a fin stack's base plate reaches a cell Reynolds number of about 90, at the same step on the CPU and the GPU (details on #642 and #661). A subgrid closure is the standard way lattice Boltzmann reaches such speeds on practical grids.

**What.** A Smagorinsky eddy viscosity in the CPU lattice solver (`crates/lbm`), opt-in per fluid step.
- **Momentum:**
  - ν_t = (C_s Δ)² |S|, with the strain rate taken locally from the non-equilibrium momentum flux each cell already has. The regularised collision computes `P = Π^neq + ½(uF + Fu) ≈ −2ρ c_s² τ S`.
  - That makes the relaxation time a per-cell closed form with no extra neighbour access: τ = ½(τ₀ + √(τ₀² + 18√2 C_s² |P| / ρ)), in lattice units, from S. Hou, J. Sterling, S. Chen, G. D. Doolen, *A lattice Boltzmann subgrid model for high Reynolds number flows*, Fields Inst. Commun. 6:151–166, 1996.
  - Built on the recursive regularised collision, as in O. Malaspinas, P. Sagaut, *Consistent subgrid scale modelling for lattice Boltzmann methods*, J. Fluid Mech. 700:514–542, 2012.
- **Heat:** with a thermal lattice, the turbulent diffusivity α_t = ν_t / Pr_t (Pr_t ≈ 0.85–0.9) is added to the scalar lattice's relaxation per cell. Otherwise the temperature lattice runs at the same high cell Péclet numbers. That means one stored ν_t (or τ) per fluid cell.
- **Model and commands:** a step setting, for example `"turbulence": {"type": "smagorinsky", "constant": 0.1, "prandtl": 0.9}` (or a collision value), with reply fields for the largest eddy viscosity ratio ν_t/ν. Off by default, so every current result stays bit for bit. The TRT collision refuses it clearly, or it's defined for TRT too.
- Cited in the module docs and in the literature list. No code of any LES or lattice Boltzmann package is read.

**Verification (docs/verification.md, `tests/oracle/` where it fits):**
- Off: all current tests and fixtures unchanged.
- Laminar: Poiseuille or Couette, where |S| is known, gives the closed-form ν_t, and the profile follows the effective viscosity.
- Taylor–Green decay: the energy decays at the effective viscosity's rate.
- A case the plain scheme can't hold (a lid-driven cavity or channel at high cell Reynolds number) stays stable, with a published reference where one fits.
- Heat: a heated channel where α_t follows ν_t / Pr_t.
- Hostile parameters: a negative, huge or NaN constant is refused.

**Done when** the CPU solver runs the #642 card (0.36–0.5 mm cells, 2–3 m/s into the intake) to steady state with the closure on, and the checks above pass.

The GPU port is a separate issue. Part of #642's path to real fan speeds; related to #157.
